I would just reiterate the point I was making with the quote from Frantz Fanon in terms of the responsibility of each generation to just through relative obscurity, because that's what we're going through now, relative obscurity, to discover its mission, fulfill it, or betray it. And for those of us who are old, like all these gray hairs like me, to be able to communicate with the younger generation and that sort of dialogue has to happen. When I was a young person, that was going on, but there seem to be very many divisions now in terms of people even being able to communicate with each other. So I think it's the task of those of us who are older to be able to speak with younger people and those who are younger to be open to listening, because I think it's going to require that intergenerational exchange and learning of energy and creativity and vision that will enable us to change the situation. So it presents an opportunity. It's a present, sometimes obstacles present opportunities, and the obstacles we face now are opportunities for us to overcome them. And when you study history, you understand that things which at some times seemed impossible, seemed that way until they were done. When black people were in chattel slavery, there were many folks who said, we can't get out of this. And Harriet Tubman showed them not only could they get out of it, but that they could get out of it and they could destroy it. So I think that's the lessons that we have to communicate and come together and move on. Thank you.
Thank you, Roger. I do agree with you. The intergenerational communication is important. Thank you. I now give the floor to Joe, please.

Thank you. As I mentioned in my previous statement, we steward different, with three different plantation sites. One of those sites is called the Woodland Plantation. And that site is the site of the largest slave revolt that happened in the United States. When I'm working on that site, I have to contemplate that history. But there's also other parts of the history that exist on the site as well, and one is. of a musician by the name of Kid Ory. He was eight years old when he started his very first band. He was a descendant of the enslaved at Woodland Plantation. Now, maybe you have not heard of the musician Kid Ory, but perhaps you've heard of one of his proteges, who's Louis Armstrong. It was Kid Ory who first hired Louis Armstrong to play in his band, and it's Kid Ory who's believed to actually have bought Louis Armstrong his first trumpet. And so I think about Kid Ory as an eight-year-old, and starting a band and all the organization and even building his own instruments and having that creativity and that freedom to dream and create his own music. And I think about our youth and what's happening in our country, particularly the black youth in the south, that their minds are being captured by industry, that our school systems aren't allowing them to create their own music and to make those connections that Kid Ory did that gave us the gift of Louis Armstrong, including himself. And so our work is really to show them that they can dream, that can create their own music, they can dance to the beat of their own drum, and they in turn can also protect their environment. They can break away from this legacy of pollution that is direct ties to the plantation system. We no longer have to be the sacrifice zones that this system has put in place for us as Afro-descendants. And so my goal is really to share more about our history, more about our art. Art, I know working in this field, we desperately need more people to be a part of these different careers. And who better than the marginalized people to be able to find and take part in their own history and be able to present it to the world. So our work will support that and I really encourage others to do the same. Thank you.
Thank you, Jill, for that really beautiful message. And lastly, Ambassador James, the floor is yours.

Thank you very much, Your Excellency. I've had tough acts to follow, but I think I will just say this. Many times, we don't understand the ways and means of the generation before us, and certainly not the generation after us. But if you look at it, the UN has been here for 81 years. The DDPA has been here for 25 years. But we are still here. And I think for a long time, my personal take is that we have been working in silos and not trying to understand each other. And I do agree with Roger that it comes time for us to have a cross-generation dialogue. A cross-generation dialogue where we, the older youth, because we move cautiously, and the younger youth can move fast, why don't we then join together so we can either move fast cautiously or cautiously fast? And this will be guided obviously by our experiences, but also make it fit for purpose for today. So my closing parting shot is, I think, join me in making the future of my daughter and her daughter the product of my very best choice. And taking forward Anatola's seed that we just planted, may we see that it grow, but for something to grow, You need to tend it. So may we tend Anatola's seed as we make the choices, our choices, the best for the generation to come. I thank you very much.
Thank you so much, Master James. Please, Anatola, quickly. Yeah.

Thank you. I love the urgent call to nurture those seeds and watch them grow. And on the subject of art and storytelling, I wanted to share one quote from Eddie S. Glaude, who writes that, "History isn't fate. "To ignore the past or to make of it a fairy tale, "or to deny it altogether will seal our fate. "Those who cannot remember the past "are condemned to repeat it. "Remembering is not sufficient to secure a better future. what and how we remember and what and who we exclude from our stories matter because those memories and stories shape how we act today and how we fight for our future. So I invite you to consider that as we tell stories of those who have historically been oppressed, those from Africa and its diaspora, and what stories can we claim our histories so that we can empower the futures we're building? Thank you.

Thank you so much. So, dear panelists, so I think, you know, we can all agree that this session has certainly been very enriching. A lot of sharing of what's been done, what has worked, and what is there more for us to do. If I could maybe just summarize a little bit. that imagination is infrastructure. And before, so before any institution can change, the public has to first be able to picture a different outcome. And that is the work of the storytelling that Anatalla's been talking about, you know, media and creative technology is just as important as it is the work of policy. And two different vantage points that we heard from Roger and Joe making the same point that participation without resourcing is not really participation. So whether it's a seat in the Human Rights Council or in the Plastics Treaty negotiations, young people and frontline communities are too often invited, but perhaps has to be more meaningful in being able to shape what happens there. you know, and but I think at the end of the of it all, Ambassador James presence here in itself is a closing point and none of what we discussed today needs a new mechanism. The Durban Working Group is already exists to receive it and the task ahead is to root today's energy into that machinery rather than build a parallel one. So, thank you so much to the incredible panelists on the table sharing your profound insights, expertise, vision, and vision for us today. I wish we had more time, but I hope this conversation does not stop here. So I now hereby close the panel. And before I do, please join me to give a round of applause for the panels. So, Excellency, the floor is back to you. Thank you.

I thank Her Excellency, Ms. Hirani, for skillfully moderating this important discussion. I also thank our distinguished panelists, distinguished speakers for the invaluable contributions and for highlighting the vital role of youth leadership in mobilizing public support and advancing the full and effective implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. Thank you again very much. We shall now continue the general debate of the high-level meeting. I would like to remind the speakers that the statements are limited to three minutes when speaking in a national capacity and five minutes when speaking on behalf of group of states. Participants with longer statements are encouraged to deliver a shorter version of the text and submit the full statement to the Secretariat. Bearing in mind the time limits, I appeal to speakers to deliver their statements at a reasonable pace so that interpretation into the official languages of the United Nations may be provided properly. I appeal for the cooperation of all distinguished speakers in observing the time limits so that all those inscribed may be heard during the time allotted. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Eritrea.

Mr. President, 25 years ago, the international community reached a landmark consensus in Durban, recognizing that racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance are fundamental violations of human dignity.

Yet today.

This scourge persists, millions of people continue to experience racial discrimination, bias, and structural inequalities. We must confront the hard truth that racism, discrimination, systematic inequalities, and neocolonialism structures are the enduring legacies of slavery, colonialism, and exploitation that continue to impact the Global South. Eritrea echoes the call for preparatory justice, emphasizing that addressing these historical wrongs through reparations, the restitution of cultural assets, and the dismantling of structural inequalities is essential to restoring dignity and building a more equitable international order. Mr. President, mobilizing global public support for the fall and the effective implementation of the declaration requires political will to translate commitments made in Durban into concrete, accountable actions. First, we must strengthen national and international legacy and policy frameworks to combat systemic racism, ensuring equal access to justice, education, health, and economic opportunities for all individuals without distinction. Second, we must harness the power of education, media and public awareness to challenge deep-rooted stereotypes and foster a culture of tolerance, equality, and mutual respect. Third, Eritrea draws attention to the adverse developmental and humanitarian consequences of unilateral coercive measures. Measures that impair the economic and social development of developing countries warrant particular scrutiny in the pursuit of equality.

Development, and human dignity.

They are a glaring example of the very intolerance and systematic inequality that the Durban Declaration seeks to eliminate. Mr. President, for Eritrea, the Durban commitment to confronting the legacies of colonialism has particular historical resonance. The Eritrean people endured successive forms of colonial domination and racial discrimination and were denied the full realization of their right to self-determination for decades. The eventual realization of independence reaffirmed that equality, dignity and self-determination are inseparable principles. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Eritrea. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Barbados.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, Borbits aligns itself with the statements made on behalf of CARICOM and the Group of 77 and China, and welcomes this opportunity to reaffirm its commitment to the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action on its 25th anniversary. The Durban Declaration remains the most comprehensive framework developed by the United Nations for confronting racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. 25 years later, its purpose remains as relevant as ever. True, there has been progress. Countries have strengthened anti-discrimination laws and policies, developed national strategies, and reinforced institutions tasked with protecting equality and human rights. Yet, as the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination has cautioned, that progress has been accompanied by stagnation and backsliding. Racism persists in unequal access to education, health care, and justice, in hate speech and racial profiling, and in discrimination against migrants, minorities, and people of African descent. The challenge is also evolving. Digital technologies and artificial intelligence can now reproduce and amplify existing racial biases unless appropriate safeguards are built into their design and use. This reminds us that combating racism and inequalities cannot be a one-time undertaking. It requires sustained action in our laws, in our institutions, in our societies, and in the technologies that increasingly shape our lives. For Barbados and the wider Caribbean, implementation of the Durban Agenda must also acknowledge the enduring consequences of slavery, the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans, indentureship, and colonialism. Reparatory justice forms part of that effort, true, but so too does the broader task of dismantling both the inequalities and discriminatory structures that those histories helped to create. We therefore welcome the second International Decade for People of African Descent and the continued work of the Permanent Forum on People of African Descent. These mechanisms provide important opportunities to advance the Durban objectives of recognition, justice and development, while ensuring that people of African descent play a meaningful role in shaping the policies that affect them. 25 years after the absence of commitment, it is ensuring their development. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Barbados. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cote d'Ivoire.

President, my delegation aligns itself with the statement delivered by Burkina Faso on behalf of the Group of African States. And we wish to add the following in our national capacity. President, 25 years following the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, We must agree that progress has been made in its implementation through the actions of international mechanisms, of independent experts, and the policies and measures put in place by states, together with the support of civil society for follow-up mechanisms. Nonetheless, it must also be recognized that humanity continues to face a rise of hate speech, racism, xenophobia, and of all forms of related intolerance. For my country, the fight against these scourges cannot be disassociated from the promotion of human dignity, equality and respect for human rights. And this is why we affirm our unwavering commitment to the major international legal instruments that reflect the collective commitment of the international community to combat the historical injustices and also contemporary forms of exclusion. President Cote d'Ivoire, faithful to its tradition of hospitality, tolerance, and respect for diversity, has made living together and national cohesion the priorities of its public action. Under the leadership of His Excellency, Mr. Alassane Ouattara, President of the Republic, Our country has implemented a number of national policies in favor of reconciliation, social integration, education, and promotion of human rights. These notably include the establishment of the National Council for Human Rights and the High Authority for Audiovisual Communication with a view to contributing to raising awareness amongst the population assistance to victims and preventing racist discourse through the press or on social networks. President, my country believes that human dignity, equality and non-discrimination are fundamental principles of international human rights law and international humanitarian law, essential to the fight against racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerances. In conclusion, Cote d'Ivoire calls for a strengthening of international cooperation and for increased funding for the Office of the High Commissioner. We reaffirm our commitment to building societies that are more inclusive.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cote d'Ivoire. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Morocco.

President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, 25 years following the International Conference of Durban, our meeting today should be an opportunity to revive a collective commitment against racism, racial discrimination and xenophobia, which, far from disappearing, are being reinvented in light of the challenges of our time. Morocco is committed to combating all forms of discrimination, has made this the cornerstone of our constitution. and we enshrine the unity of the nation based on the plurality of our Amazigh, Sahrawi, Hebraic, Mediterranean, other sources. This translates into our legal framework that it is impossible to create any kind of hierarchy here. Under the rule of Mohammed VI, we have been implementing a national strategy of immigration and asylum based on a humanitarian and solidarity approach. We're also committed to religious discourse. This is a rampart against hate and intolerance. But we cannot be successful in this without the full participation of all stakeholders. nor without international cooperation, notably South-South cooperation, we once again reiterate our commitment to work alongside the international community for the full and effective implementation of the commitments made 25 years ago for a more just and fair world free of discrimination. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Morocco. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

President, 25 years ago, the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, DDPA, set the noble goal of eliminating racism in all its forms and manifestations, embedding racial justice and equality into the agenda of our times, and inspiring tireless international efforts. Over the past 25 years, the global anti-racism cause went through an extraordinary journey. However, some long-standing problems remain unresolved, such as colonialism, neo-Nazism, and racial discrimination in their contemporary forms, all of which pose real threats to the fundamental rights and world peace and development. Looking into the future, we must strictly uphold the spirit of DDPA, forge strong synergy, and join hands to build a world of equality for all. First, peace and tranquility must be maintained. Survival and safety of life are the foundation for enjoying human rights. We must abide by the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, resolve international disputes and hotspot issues through peaceful means, and prevent and combat race or religion-based violence and hate crimes in conflicts. Second, common development should be the focus. Bridging the gap in development is crucial for eliminating the breeding ground of racism. It is imperative to accelerate the implementation of the 2030 agenda, reduce inequality in development within and between countries, ensure fair access by ethnic minorities to development opportunities and benefits, and promote social justice and inclusive growth. Third, dialogue among civilizations must be promoted. Diversity in civilization drives progress. We must promote the shared values of humanity, advocate exchanges, mutual learning, and harmony in diversity among different races and civilizations, and prevent emerging technologies from fueling radical ideologies, xenophobia, and hate speeches. Fourth, multilateral collaboration must be enhanced. Eliminating racism is a shared responsibility for all. We must strengthen global anti-racism governance, fully implement the relevant international conventions and the resolutions of GA and Human Rights Council, take concrete actions to correct the historical injustice towards Africa, and oppose double standard in combating racism. As an old saying goes, ever diligent and ever in pace with the times, China actively supports and participates in all international efforts against racism. We stand ready to work with all parties, reaffirm our commitment to DDPA, and advance toward a community with a shared future for mankind. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of China. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mozambique.

Mr. President, despite the progress made over the past quarter century, racism and racial discrimination persist in our society and institutions. Africans and people of African descent continue to face systemic inequalities, discrimination, and exclusion. emerging challenges, particularly those associated with digital technologies and artificial intelligence, risk reproducing and amplifying these racial biases at a scale. For Mozambique, the full and effective implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action requires an honest acknowledgement of the history and its enduring consequences. An equitable future cannot be built on buried truths. Sadly, the trafficking of enslaved Africans, slavery and colonialism inflicted profound human suffering, and the repercussions of structural inequality continue to affect people of African descent across generations. Mr. President, the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration coincides with the early years of the second international decade for the people of African descent under the theme recognition, justice, and development. In my capacity as facilitator of the consultation on the possible update of the program of activities for the implementation of the international decade for the people of African descent, I had the privilege of listening to the views of member states and relevant stakeholders on how to strengthen the implementation of the second international decade. One message has emerged clearly from this dialogue. The Durban agenda and international decades are not parallel efforts, they are mutually reinforcing. Durban is not as historical text to be commemorated. It must become a living agenda. Its 25th anniversary should serve as a bridge between historical recognition and contemporary action, between the commitments made in 2001 and the challenges confronting our society today. Mr. President, as we look toward the next 25 years, our collective responsibility is clear, to transform recognition into justice, justice into development, and our commitments into tangible change in the lives of present and future generations. The second International Decade must not repeat the patterns of commemoration without implementation. It must deliver measurable progress on reparatory justice, on data-driven accountability, on equitable representation in the digital economy.
I thank the distinguished representative of Mozambique. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malaysia.

Malaysia also wishes to express its appreciation to the Permanent Representatives of Brunei Darussalam and Zimbabwe for their able stewardship and tireless efforts in co-facilitating the negotiations on the Political Declaration. 25 years ago, the global community forged a historic blueprint to combat racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. As we commemorate this milestone, we must confront a sobering reality: old structures of prejudice persist, while intolerance has evolved into modern manifestations, including digital hate speech, religious profiling, and Islamophobia. The deliberate targeting of civilians, health systems, and critical humanitarian infrastructure are horrific and abhorrent. Israel must be held accountable for grave violations of international law and crimes against humanity. Mr. President, As a multicultural nation, Malaysia attaches fundamental importance to social cohesion. Guided by Malaysia Madani and our national principles, our domestic policies nurture unity in diversity. We recognize that social harmony requires inclusive, equitable, and sustainable economic development, supported by good governance and legal protection for all. Yet, challenges remain. Beyond economic gaps and digital hate speech, we must address deep-seated structural and systemic barriers that perpetuate inequality. For Malaysia, these challenges are calls to action. We seek to address the root causes of prejudice through structural economic equity and sound policies including the national unity policy and the 13 Malaysia plan we urge the international community to move beyond pronouncements and embed anti-racism principles into governance by fostering community-led integration ensuring fairness in digital spheres and dismantling systemic bias we can build a future where diversity is celebrated and equality is lived reality in conclusion Malaysia reaffirms its strong commitment to the full and effective implementation of the DDPA, we stand in firm solidarity with global efforts to address historical injustices and structural inequalities. Let us translate our commitments into tangible and inclusive policies. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Iraq.

President, we align ourselves with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of the G77 and China. And we welcome the holding of this high-level meeting to mark the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. We reiterate our commitment to combat racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance in all of their forms. 25 years following the adoption of the DDPA, it continues to be the international framework for overcoming these challenges. This is an opportunity for us to renew our commitment and to translate them into national, regional, and international measures that are effective. We underscore the importance of combating the manifestations of racism, racial discrimination, discrimination, hate speech, and intolerance based on religion or ethnic origin, including Islamophobia. The vulnerable and fragile situation of migrants or refugees and other displaced persons is Particularly significant, we have seen in my country a large-scale situation of displacement, and we are very cognizant of the need to protect refugees and displaced persons in light of the different forms of discrimination and xenophobia. These individuals must be treated in line with the international conventions. Furthermore, new technologies pose new challenges. AI and digital platforms can contribute to development, education, and to the inclusion of all persons. Nonetheless, the creation and the use of such technologies can actually lead to greater bias, discrimination, and inequality. And this is why we call for international cooperation so that we can strengthen human rights and ensure they are respected in the digital sphere. Furthermore, we are aware of the critical role that young people play in terms of participating on an equal footing with others in order to ensure more effective policies to manage the digital sphere and to combat racism and racial discrimination. The Republic of Iraq wishes to reiterate that diversity is a source of strength and unity rather than of division. This is why it is necessary to continue to ensure that dialogue exists between peoples and religions, and there is a need to ensure that the dignity of each individual is respected. And this is why we have instituted a number of measures to implement the Durban Declaration. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Iraq. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Angola.

Thank you very much, Mr. President, distinguished delegates. Angola is honored to participate in this high-level meeting commemorating the 25th anniversary of the adoption of Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. Angola aligns with the African Group and the G77 plus China. These milestones offer an opportunity to recognize the progress made and renew our commitment to eradicating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. Adopted in 2001, the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action remains a fundamental framework It is especially significant for its recognition and the enduring consequences of slavery, the transatlantic slave trade, and colonialism for Africa and people of African descent. 25 years on, renewed manifestations of racism and intolerance threaten the progress achieved. On 25th March, Africa and the world reached a historic milestone with the adoption of General Assembly Resolution 80/250. The resolution declares the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialized chattel enslavement of Africans to be the gravest crime against humanity and calls for institutional accountability and reparatory justice. Excellencies, for Angola, this cause is deeply rooted in our own history. The Angolan people's struggle against colonialism was also a struggle for freedom, self-determination, dignity, equality, and fundamental rights. Angola therefore reaffirms these principles of Durban and the need to address the historical legacies of slavery, colonialism, and systemic racism. We support dialogue on the effective measures to redress historical injustice, promote reconciliation, and advance greater justice and equality. Angola welcomes the work of United Nations mechanisms combating racism and racial discrimination.
I thank the distinguished President. I thank the distinguished representative of Angola. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cabo Verde.

President, Cabo Verde aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the African Group and the G77 and China, and welcomes the convening of this high-level meeting. Coming together is a beginning, staying together is progress, and working together is success. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cabo Verde. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kenya.

Thank you, Mr. President. Twenty-five years ago, Member States of the United Nations adopted the Dapag Declaration and Program of Action as a comprehensive framework for confronting racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. Today, We meet not only to commemorate this achievement, but also to assess the progress made and renew our resolve to translate this commitment into practical protection, effective remedies, and accountability. For it is but Kenya reaffirms its commitment to the TDDPA. Our efforts are grounded in our constitution. and it is guarantees of equality, human dignity, non-discrimination, and the protection of minorities and marginalized groups. We recognize that the measure of our commitment lies not only in the standards we proclaim, but also in the institutions we build, the remedies we provide, and the lived experience of affected persons and communities. This commitment is reflected in practical action. The National Cohesion and Integration Act remains central to Kenya's efforts to promote national cohesion and integration and to address ethnic and racial discrimination, hate speech, ethnic contempt and related conduct that threaten peace coexistence. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Kenya. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nepal.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, 25 years ago in Durban, the international community united with a solemn resolve to confront racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and the enduring legacies of colonialism, apartheid, and systemic injustice. Today, that promise remains an urgent moral imperative. Prejudice and exclusion still constrain human potential while morphing into digital spaces and algorithmic bias. As Nelson Mandela reminded us, hatred is learned. This also implies our societies can intentionally cultivate dignity, empathy, and mutual respect. Nepal's progressive constitution guarantees equality before the law, prohibits discrimination in all spheres, and mandates proportional inclusion for historically marginalized communities. These domestic guarantees reflect our global commitments as a state party to seven core international human rights treaties, including ICERD. To accelerate the Durban Programme of Action, we urge four priorities. First, legal and civic action, enforcing robust anti-discrimination laws while instilling human rights education across school. Second, empowering marginalized voices, ensuring historically oppressed communities meaningfully co-design public policy. Third, governing emerging technology, regulating artificial intelligence to eliminate racial algorithms and hate speech. And finally, principled multilateralism, deepening global cooperation to eradicate systemic intolerances worldwide. True human progress rests upon the inviolable dignity of every individual. Thank you, and
I thank the distinguished Minister of Nepal. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Guatemala.

This commemoration represents an opportunity for us to renew our commitment to their effective implementation through dialogue, cooperation, and concrete actions that allow us to advance towards more inclusive and equitable societies. Guatemala reaffirms the importance of promoting recognition and justice and development of the Maya, Garifuna, Xinca and Afro-descendant peoples, as well as guaranteeing their full and meaningful participation in decisions concerning them. We will continue to strengthen spaces for intercultural dialogue and institutional actions aimed at combating racism and racial discrimination, and to broadening access to education, health, justice, and opportunities for development, with special attention to women and young people. We must continue to be attentive to new challenges. Digital technologies and AI offer significant opportunities for development. Their development and use should promote equality and be accompanied by safeguards based on human rights and non-discrimination. Furthermore, as my delegation has maintained in prior commemorations, we hold a firm position when we point out that Anti-Semitism, while it is not recognized in the text, constitutes one of the forms of intolerance with a growing trend, and we should remain vigilant so that we do not recommit the errors of the past. Guatemala reiterates its full readiness to continue contributing constructively to the full implementation of the D-DPA. This is the only way for us to build more just, inclusive, and peaceful societies. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Guatemala, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Suriname.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, 25 years after the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, its message remains urgent and personal. My country has been shaped by slavery and colonialism. People were brought to our shores on the systems that denied their humanity, exploited their labour, and left consequences that did not disappear with the abolition of slavery or the achievement of independence.

Today,

Suriname is a sovereign and diverse nation built by the descendants of people who endured, resisted, and survived. That history gives us a responsibility to move forward.
